correctness.rationale: For a fixed quadratic K, the all-ideal norm coefficients are 1*chi_D. Splitting the corresponding pair sum at sqrt(y), bounded partial sums of chi_D give O_K(sqrt(y)) on the large-character-index portion and on the tail replacing the partial L(1,chi_D); flooring on the remaining part has the same error. This verifies the stated all-ideal estimate for real as well as imaginary quadratic K. The squarefree count follows by ideal Möbius inversion: the omitted N(J)^-2 tail is O_K(y^-1/2) and the accumulated errors are bounded by sqrt(y) times a harmonic norm sum. Abel summation of the all-ideal main term plus residual gives the claimed constant at sigma=2/3, since the integral of the residual continues zeta_K(s)-rho_K s/(s-1) into Re(s)>1/2; the analogous squarefree tail calculation gives 2 kappa_K Y^-1/2. Splitting exponents at each prime ideal by parity makes I=A²B³ unique with B squarefree and no coprimality condition. For T=x^1/5 all pairs lie in the union of the two strip counts, with a full overlap rectangle. The leading terms of size x^2/5 have coefficients -2,+3,-1 times rho_K*kappa_K and cancel. The remaining error sizes are x^1/2 T^-1 log(2T), x^1/4 T^1/4, x^1/3 T^-1/6, x^1/6 T^2/3 log(2x), and T^3/2 log(2T), all O_K(x^3/10 log(2x)). The Gaussian coefficient sign follows from positive alternating beta and eta at 2/3 and the negative factor 1-2^(1-2/3) converting eta to zeta. The unit ideal is included, real noninteger cutoffs use weak inequalities, and no claim of nonvanishing for general K is needed. The frozen checker was inspected, not executed; its finite Gaussian counts do not prove the asymptotic.

value.rationale: The previous leading estimate leaves an entire natural secondary scale unresolved. The explicit second term and power-saving remainder distinguish a real arithmetic effect, including a definite negative secondary correction for the Gaussian field, rather than just shortening a remainder at an arbitrary exponent. The proof explains the cancellation that makes this second term measurable, across both real and imaginary quadratic fields.
